enrichment.markdown:
- **Arie Dushnik and his family.** The strongest outside addition is a family link in the book’s memorial section: Zeev Virobnik was Arie Dushnik’s grandson, born in Tel Aviv to Zelig Virobnik and Leah Edel Dushnik. The account describes Zeev’s business-school education and government work, and says he was killed defending Kibbutz Negba on June 2, 1948. It gives no further biographical details about Arie himself, so his dates, occupation, and later life remain unconfirmed. [JewishGen, pp. 277–278](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/david-gorodek/dav275.html)

- **The committee and its associates.** A related source identifies **Hana Spielberg-Grenadier**—apparently the supplied Hannah Spielberg-Grandir under a different transliteration—as a major contributor to the David-Horodok Women’s Organization in Detroit. It also names **Yakov Kitai** (likely the supplied Y. Kitai) as an organizer of the New York association who gathered material and funds for the memorial book. These passages establish community-organization work, but do not establish that either person belonged to the Israel committee or the Gemach fund. [JewishGen, introduction](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/Davyd-Haradok/dav001.html)

- **A. Gliniansky, Elijah and Isaac Gliniansky, Samuel Tsatsik, and Y. Kitai.** I found no independently verifiable biographical or family records for the Gliniansky names or Tsatsik in the permitted archive searches. The memorial book’s necrology does list **Aharon and Beila Glinansky** among David-Horodok natives who died in Israel, but it does not connect them to the three supplied Gliniansky entries; the spelling resemblance alone is not enough to identify them as the same people. [JewishGen, p. 299](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/David-Gorodek/dav287.html)

- **David-Horodok, Israel, America, Russia, and the Gemach fund.** The account of the memorial book’s publication confirms that survivors organized across Israel and the diaspora, including associations in Detroit and New York. The history describes postwar migration from David-Horodok toward America and, later, other destinations; it provides context for these overseas networks, not proof of the named committee members’ own migration histories. The supplied record’s “Russia” reference should also be read cautiously: David-Horodok’s political borders changed, and the history says it belonged to Russia until 1920, then Poland until September 1939. I found no separate archive evidence documenting the David-Horodok Martyrs’ Gemach Fund’s activities or membership. [JewishGen, introduction](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/Davyd-Haradok/dav001.html); [JewishGen, town history](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/Davyd-Haradok/dav001.html)

Searches across the permitted JewishGen material used Dushnik/Dushnick, Gliniansky/Glinansky, Tsatsik, Spielberg/Spielberg-Grenadier, Kitai, and combinations with David-Horodok, Israel, New York, Detroit, and Gemach. I did not find corroborating individual records in the accessible results for several of these names; that absence is not evidence that they had no family or community history.
